lessons.title: Calling SDK versus Call Automation
lessons.why: One is a person in a browser. The other is your service answering the call.
body: The Calling SDK is the client for a human on a web or mobile page. Call Automation is the server API that answers, plays, recognizes, and transfers, and then receives events. A page that only uses the client SDK will not run an IVR.
If your app never sees the events, the call can be up while your code is asleep. Log the event type and the call id. Event Grid is one delivery path. A missed subscription looks like a broken prompt.

chart.title: Pick one primary
chart.note: You may use both, for different jobs.

lessons.say: Call Automation is the server-side IVR. The Calling SDK is a person in the browser.
lessons.fault: The app never answers, so the caller hears ringing until the platform gives up.
lessons.listen: Use Call Automation when a bot answers, and make sure the events actually reach your app.

lessons.title: Teams interop from ACS
lessons.why: A bot that can dial the PSTN and cannot reach a Teams expert is half an IVR.
body: ACS can be configured to call Teams users and to join Teams meetings when the interop prerequisites are met. A raw ACS identity is not a Teams user. Follow the current interop article for the resource you created.
The transfer target still needs to be able to receive the call. In a Teams estate that means Teams Phone and a number when the call is PSTN. Test the transfer, not only the prompt.

chart.title: Interop is extra setup
chart.note: Not implied by owning both products.

lessons.say: ACS does not automatically become a Teams user. I follow the interop article and I test the transfer.
lessons.fault: The bot dials the PSTN and cannot transfer to a Teams expert.
lessons.listen: Set up ACS and Teams interop on purpose, then test a transfer to a real Teams user.

lessons.title: An IVR as events
lessons.why: The call is a sequence of events. If you cannot name them, you cannot debug them.
body: A small flow is answer, play, recognize DTMF or speech, then transfer or hang up. Recognize needs a timeout. Digit 0, or an equivalent, should always reach a human. Hang-up is a complete design only when the caller did not need a person.
The lab on this campus is that sequence without a cloud subscription. Production adds the event subscription, the speech resource if you use one, and the queue you transfer to.
lessons.say: Answer, play, recognize, transfer. The escape is tested every time the prompt changes.
lessons.fault: The recognize step has no escape and the caller is trapped.
lessons.listen: Treat the IVR as events: answer, play, recognize, and a tested transfer to a human.

lessons.title: Azure AI Speech
lessons.why: Speech-to-text and text-to-speech are services with their own language, voice, and approval rules.
body: Azure AI Speech can transcribe the caller and synthesize the prompt. The language of the prompt has to match the caller or every intent becomes unknown. A custom neural voice has approval rules. Do not assume you can clone a person.
Log the recognition result beside the call id. When the bot is wrong, you need the text it thought it heard, not a feeling.

chart.title: Speech is not the phone system
chart.note: It plugs into the recognize step.

lessons.say: I pick a voice I am allowed to use, match the language, and log what the recognizer heard.
lessons.fault: The prompt language does not match the caller and every intent is unknown.
lessons.listen: Azure AI Speech can talk and listen. It is not emergency calling, and you log what it thought it heard.

lessons.title: Copilot Studio voice
lessons.why: The agent people mean is often a Copilot Studio bot on the contact-center voice channel.
body: Classic topics are a menu you can test. Generative orchestration chooses a path and needs tighter bounds. Either way, ground the bot in knowledge sources you trust, and keep a human escape that does not depend on the model feeling cooperative.

Do not put this bot on the emergency number. Do not make it the only target of the public number unless overflow to a queue is real and tested. A keyword lab on this campus is a stand-in, not a model call.
lessons.say: The voice agent has sources I trust and an escape I tested. It does not own emergency calls.
lessons.fault: The agent is the only target of the public number, including emergencies.
lessons.listen: Copilot Studio can front the voice channel if it is grounded and can always reach a human. Keep it off the emergency route.

lessons.title: Foundry, and what not to invent
lessons.why: Azure AI Foundry is where you evaluate a model. It does not route PSTN, and it used to be called Azure AI Studio.
body: Use Foundry, or the current Azure AI project experience, to evaluate prompts against questions whose answers you already know. A model change that ships to a phone number without an evaluation is an outage you chose.
Do not invent unannounced voice features. A future hook in this campus is a seam you can build today: an event, an identifier, a queue overflow. It is not a rumor about a product roadmap.

flow.label: Ship
flow.detail: To a queue that can overflow

lessons.say: I evaluate the model before it touches a phone number, and I do not design around unannounced features.
lessons.fault: A prompt change reaches the IVR on Friday with no test set.
lessons.listen: Use Azure AI Foundry to evaluate a model. Do not pretend it is a phone system, and do not invent roadmap items.
